items.title: A estética do cotidiano nos jogos digitais contemporâneos: as banalidades presentes em grand theft auto V
items.author: Perini, Henrique Araújo
items.note: Covers Spacewar! in a history of digital games: MIT origin, space race and E. E. Smith as inspiration, inertia and gravity, its visual representation, and Computer Space by Bushnell and Dabney. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 98-101.

items.title: Computer Liberation. Zur Imaginationsgeschichte der Computer- und Netzwerkkultur, 1960-2000
items.author: Frick, Jonas
items.note: Imaginationsgeschichte of computer culture. Discusses Russell drawing on E. E. Smith for Spacewar and reads Brand's Rolling Stone article, including its echo of Kerouac, as a report on the new research centres. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 29, 108 and after.

items.title: Інформаційна система аналізу ринку комп'ютерних ігор
items.author: Анісімов, Олексій Юрійович
items.in: Institutional Repository of National University of Food Technologies
items.note: Ukrainian thesis whose history of computer games describes Spacewar! on the PDP-1 by Russell, Graetz and Wiitanen, with the additions by Edwards, and its wide distribution. Spacewar! at p. 186 (PDF p. 2).

items.title: Cybersport as a Phenomenon of Digital Media Culture
items.author: Тахтамишева, Катерина Олександрівна; Takhtamysheva, K.
items.in: Electronic Kharkiv National University Institutional Repository (Kharkiv National University)
items.publisher: V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University
items.note: Ukrainian thesis on cybersport giving the 1972 Intergalactic Spacewar Olympics as first esports event and the origin of the game with Russell in 1962. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 16-19.

items.title: Chatbots As Fluent Polyglots: Revisiting Breakthrough Code Snippets
items.author: Noever, David A.; Kevin, Williams,
items.note: Asks ChatGPT to explain the PDP-1 assembly of Spacewar as its first task, with a code excerpt and the model's description of the needle and the wedge.

items.title: Los videojuegos también son de nosotras. Videojuegos analizados desde una perspectiva de género
items.author: Romero Mora, Elvira
items.note: Undergraduate thesis. Subsection on the first reproducible videogame: Russell saw games as entertainment, gravity affected missiles, then Bill Pitts used the PDP-11 to bring it to arcades. Spacewar! at PDF p. 11.

items.title: Arquitectura y videojuegos: relaciones
items.author: Díaz-Vázquez, Pilar
items.note: Treats Spacewar! in timelines of computer graphics and games, compares its vector display with Computer Space's bitmapped approach, and links it to Sketchpad-era graphics. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 55, 67-68, 129-130.

items.title: Space ShooterPolygon 2D: um resgate nostálgico
items.author: De Melo Ferreira, Thiago
items.publisher: Programa de Historia das Ciencias e das Tecnicas e Epistemologia
items.note: Portuguese paper on a 2D shooter that treats Spacewar and Space Invaders as exemplars of the shoot-em-up, describing Russell's game at MIT. Spacewar! at PDF p. 2.

items.title: Ecomods: An Ecocritical Approach to Game Modification // Ecomods: Una aproximación ecocrítica a la modificación de los videojuegos
items.author: Bohunicky, Kyle Matthew
items.in: Ecozon@: European Journal of Literature, Culture and Environment
items.note: Reports Christiansen's argument that Spacewar! (1962) was the first game mod and describes Russell and the MIT hackers in that light.

items.title: Análisis de la retronarratividad como fundamento de la comunicación y la estética videolúdica
items.author: Martin Rodríguez, Iván
items.note: Doctoral thesis. Compares rival first-game claims, where Spacewar! counts as first or third, and argues its ship as avatar and science fiction theme hold features of later games, a case of retronarrativity. Spacewar! at PDF p. 32.

items.title: JUMPs durch exotische Zonen. Portale, Hyperräume und Teleportation in Computern und Computerspielen
items.author: Höltgen, Stefan
items.note: Section Adressen: 1961-1981 Spacewar! treats the founding legend at MIT, the programming challenge reported by Levy, the star map via Pias, and the hyperspace cheat, as the start of its history of jumps through code. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 7-8.

items.title: Reconstructing WARRIOR: Vectorbeams, Natural Magick & Business Intrigue
items.author: Rousse, Thomas H.
items.in: Kinephanos, Cultural History of Video Games special issue
items.note: A section traces the line from Spacewar! at MIT to Larry Rosenthal and Cinematronics via Computer Space, correcting claims in Kent about Rosenthal, his thesis and vector graphics. Spacewar! at 158 onward.

items.title: Violencia, psicología y videojuegos = Violence, psychology and video-game: historia de una relación controvertida = history of a problematic relationship /
items.author: Pérez-Fernández, F.; Mampaso Desbrow, Joanne; Corbí Gran, Beatriz; Martín-Moreno Blasco, C.
items.in: Edupsykhé. Revista de Psicología y Educación
items.note: Spanish history of violence and psychology in games that describes Russell's Spacewar! on the PDP-1 as first video game in the strict sense.

items.title: BALALU: Anticipar los cambios en un Software OA
items.author: Fuentes Zamorano, Cecilia Andrea; Casas, Sandra Isabel
items.publisher: Universidad Nacional de la Patagonia Austral
items.note: Spanish report on change impact analysis using Spacewar, the example program shipped with AspectJ for Eclipse, as a study case. Not the 1962 code.

items.title: Videojuegos para la transformación social. Aportaciones conceptuales y metodológicas.
items.author: González, Carlos
items.note: Spanish thesis on games for social change, with a figure and passage on Spacewar! as what most specialists take as the first modern video game. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 20, 90-92.

items.title: Tirando del ovillo de la Red: matrices culturales en el origen de Internet
items.author: Cabello Fernández-Delgado, Florencio
items.note: History of the Internet's cultural matrices. Takes Russell and Spacewar as the first of its hacker cases, stressing the wave of successive improvements, then Galaxy Game at Stanford and Bushnell's Computer Space. Spacewar! at PDF p. 11.

items.title: A interface e o videogame: articulações semióticas
items.author: Rocha, Cleomar; Galiza, Bruno
items.note: Portuguese article on interface and video game semiotics, arguing Spacewar by Russell is properly the first video game because of how it represents and allows interaction. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 4, 5, 8.

items.title: Análisis del contexto histórico y tecnológico del origen de los videojuegos.
items.author: López Nieto, Daniel
items.in: Revista ICONO14. Revista científica de Comunicación y Tecnologías emergentes
items.note: Spanish historical account of video game origins with a passage on Spacewar: Russell and friends at MIT in 1961, the PDP-1, and an image of the original. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 5-6.

items.title: FROM THE BALL OF THE NET: CULTURAL FRAMEWORKS IN THE ORIGIN OF INTERNET
items.author: Fernández-Delgado, Florencio Cabello
items.in: Argumentos de razón técnica: Revista española de ciencia, tecnología y sociedad, y filosofía de la tecnología
items.note: Spanish article on cultural origins of the internet covering Russell's Spacewar, its display of two ships, and Bushnell meeting it at Utah before Computer Space.

items.title: Breve historia de los videojuegos
items.author: Belli, Simone; López, Cristian
items.note: Says Russell spent six months on Spacewar! with vector graphics on a PDP-1, the first with some success, and treats Galaxy War and Bushnell's Computer Space of 1971 as versions of it. Spacewar! at PDF p. 4.

items.title: Into the social factory: an investigation into labour & value in the video-games industry
items.author: Rodgers, Thomas Arthur
items.note: Ph.D. Places Spacewar! at the intersection of the hacker ethic and military-funded Cold War research, via Kline et al., and explains that the $120,000 PDP-1 ruled out commercial sale. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 102-103.

items.title: Respawn: Gamers, Hackers, and Technogenic Life
items.author: Milburn, Colin
items.note: Figure 1.1 and opening discussion of Brand on hackers making Spacewar; notes cite Graetz, Levy and Turkle on its role in hacking, list its authors and address its public-domain status.

items.title: Computer game worlds
items.author: Pias, Claus
items.note: Contents list a section 'Spacewar' between the TX-0 and Sensorama in the chapter on action games. It credits Kotok, Samson and Russell, quotes Brand that hackers made it, and has a figure of 1960s hackers playing in 1983.

items.title: The friendly orange glow: the untold story of the PLATO system and the dawn of cyberculture
items.author: Dear, Brian
items.note: Separates PLATO's Spacewar from MIT's 1962 program, says what puts MIT's version in the histories, and contrasts its PDP-1 console display with PLATO's graphics constraint. Spacewar! at 226-229.

items.title: Wonderland: how play made the modern world
items.author: Johnson, Steven
items.note: Tells how students used the PDP-1 for a game of cosmic conflict, gives its two-player rules, cites Brand's Rolling Stone piece and Graetz, and includes a plate of Edwards and Samson playing. Spacewar! at 198-201.

items.title: Rise of the machines: a cybernetic history
items.author: Rid, Thomas
items.note: Recounts Brand's Rolling Stone piece: Spacewar as the first computer video game, Brand calling it a crystal ball and heresy, and the tinkerers he portrayed, set beside Bateson's philosophy.

items.title: A brief history of video games
items.author: Stanton, Richard
items.note: Pages on Spacewar!: conceived in 1961 by MIT students, the Needle and Wedge, gravity and moving in on the star, exposure limited by the PDP-1; photographs of Russell and of emulated play. Spacewar! at 33-35.

items.title: The cybernetics moment, or, why we call our age the information age
items.author: Kline, Ronald R.
items.note: Discusses Brand's 1972 article as a frontier of machine cybernetics: hackers playing through the night, Kay interviewed at PARC, and Kay's sketch of two children playing Spacewar on Dynabooks.

items.title: The routledge companion to video game studies
items.note: Edited by Wolf and Perron. Chapters on origins set Tennis for Two beside Spacewar!, compare their viewpoints, discuss naming it the first digital game, and contrast player-versus-player with Pong.
items.author: Wolf, Mark J. P.; Perron, Bernard

items.title: Moving innovation: a history of computer animation
items.author: Sito, Tom
items.note: In a history of animation: Russell and classmates create the game, the naming, DEC shipping it as a free demo, Bushnell unable to afford a $120,000 PDP-1 for his version, and terms its inventors recorded.

items.title: War play: video games and the future of armed conflict
items.author: Mead, Corey
items.note: Section 'Spacewar! and Beyond' traces military game roots to it: invented in 1962 by 23-year-old Russell and colleagues, E. E. Smith as his main influence, its star charts and PDP-1 interface; includes a photograph. Spacewar! at 14.

items.title: Atari Inc.: business is fun
items.author: Goldberg, Marty
items.note: DEC left it running on delivered PDP-1s; by 1969 hackers had taken it far beyond MIT. Bushnell plans to charge players for it, and Ampex colleagues saw it at Stanford's AI lab. Separate from Cinematronics Space War mentions.

items.title: Playing at the world: a history of simulating wars, people and fantastic adventures, from chess to role-playing games
items.author: Peterson, Jon
items.note: Traces 1960s wargame hobbyist discussion: Andrews's inquiry in Gamesman about its origins, a March 1968 reply from MIT on difficulty of mainframe gaming, and Computer Space as its adaptation by Bushnell and Dabney.

items.title: The golden age of video games: the birth of a multi-billion dollar industry
items.author: Dillon, Roberto
items.note: Part 1 'The Beginning' shows a match and tells of Russell and friends programming it, improvements by Kotok and Saunders, Bushnell among its players, and Dutch Goose customers who had played it at Stanford.

items.title: Replay: the history of video games
items.author: Donovan, Tristan
items.note: Opening history: Graetz on choosing spaceships, the two-player duel, control boxes replacing the PDP-1's 18 switches, completion by spring 1962, and Tuck's coin-operated Galaxy Game; also a gameography entry.

items.title: Racing the beam: the Atari Video computer system
items.author: Montfort, Nick
items.note: Recurrent comparison: Bushnell discovering it at Utah, its 1962 PDP-1 display, two-player structure against Atari VCS design, and its relation to Star Castle and Space Wars. A ludography credits Russell, Graetz and Wiitanen. Spacewar! at 5, 7, 8, 31, 51-52, 84-86.

items.title: Games of empire: global capitalism and video games
items.author: Dyer-Witheford, Nick
items.note: Treats Russell's game, made on a PDP-1, as the ur-video game over Higinbotham's and Baer's, and quotes Brand on it being 'part of no one's grand scheme' and on computer power to the people.

items.title: Vintage games: an insider look at the history of Grand Theft Auto, Super Mario, and the most influential games of all time
items.author: Loguidice, Bill
items.note: Bonus chapter 'Spacewar! (1962): The Best Waste of Time in the History of the Universe'. The text compares Adventure's PDP-10 authors with its hackers on the PDP-1 and links Asteroids and Omega Race to its physics.

items.title: La saga des jeux vidéo
items.author: Ichbiah, Daniel
items.note: Describes Space War arising from the DEC PDP-1's graphics, then Bushnell's discovery of it, his addiction, imagining it in an amusement park, and returning to it while at Ampex.

items.title: Understanding video games: the essential introduction
items.author: Egenfeldt-Nielsen, Simon
items.note: History chapter: the PDP-1 led to the game, its resemblance to space battle films, its wraparound space, and Bushnell seeing financial possibilities in it. Cites Graetz.

items.title: The video game explosion: a history from PONG to Playstation and beyond
items.note: Edited by Wolf. Calls it the most famous mainframe game, by Russell, Graetz and Kotok at MIT around 1962, with hyperspace, copied and adapted across computers; also relates Cinematronics' and Vectorbeam's 1977 arcade games to it.
items.author: Wolf, Mark J. P.

items.title: From Sun Tzu to XBox: war and video games
items.author: Halter, Ed
items.note: Calls it the mainframe-era ancestor of the video game, describes the Hingham Institute fellows, Graetz's history and DECUS note, and Brand's Rolling Stone article and First Intergalactic Spacewar Olympics. Spacewar! at 141.

items.title: From counterculture to cyberculture: Stewart Brand, the Whole Earth Network, and the rise of digital utopianism
items.author: Turner, Fred
items.note: Reads Brand's Rolling Stone piece as linking computer research to New Communalist ideals: October 1972 visit with photographer Annie Leibovitz, the Intergalactic Spacewar Olympics, and hackers rather than planners making the game.

items.title: What the dormouse said--: how the sixties counterculture shaped the personal computer industry
items.author: Markoff, John
items.note: Describes the game at MIT as a classic collaborative hack, Russell's departure and the cult following, Bushnell's encounter with it, and Brand's Rolling Stone article on the computer scene. Cites Graetz.

items.title: Handbook of computer game studies
items.note: Edited by Raessens and Goldstein. Chapters treat it as a playful hack on the PDP-1 and debate whether it was the first video game; a chapter epigraph and anecdote on Russell's pinball remark.

items.title: Videogames
items.author: Newman, James (James A.)
items.note: Discusses the debated birth of videogames with Russell's Spacewar as the most cited modern case, players contending with inertia and gravity, and lists a Java version and Graetz.

items.title: Supercade: a visual history of the videogame age 1971-1984
items.author: Burnham, Van
items.note: Reprints Graetz's 'The Origin of Spacewar!' (copyright 1981, with permission), including 'The Hackers Meet Spacewar!' and the control boxes, beside a Montfort piece on TMRC and a Spacewar! game entry.

items.title: A history of modern computing
items.author: Ceruzzi, Paul E.
items.note: Uses Brand's 1972 Rolling Stone article: people at a Stanford lab playing Spacewar on a PDP-10, the game as a view of computing far from the mainframe, ahead of the personal computer.

items.title: Digital culture
items.author: Gere, Charlie
items.note: Names Spacewar as the first recorded digital computer game and first video game, by Russell and others at MIT, used to demonstrate the PDP-1 to customers and encountered by Bushnell; also cites Brand's 1972 article.

items.title: High score!: the illustrated history of electronic games
items.author: DeMaria, Rusel
items.note: Prologue on Spacewar!: Graetz's account of the brainstorm, E. E. Smith's novels as source, two rocket ships, Kotok's concurrent project, and a photograph of a PDP-1 at the Computer History Museum. Bushnell is named as an heir. Spacewar! at 12.

items.title: The medium of the video game
items.note: Wolf's history describes the game by Russell, Graetz and others on the PDP-1, its two ships, drawing on Graetz. A note on Baer's preface says PDP-1s cost $120,000 and few had access; another discusses patents.
items.author: Wolf, Mark J. P.

items.title: The ultimate history of video games: from Pong to Pokémon and beyond: the story behind the craze that touched our lives and changed the world
items.author: Kent, Steve L
items.note: Chapter 'Forgotten Fathers' opens with a Russell epigraph, then covers TMRC members revising Spacewar, dedicated control boxes on the PDP-1, and earlier interactive programs. A timeline dates the game to 1961. Spacewar! at 16.

items.title: The dream machine: J. C. R. Licklider and the revolution that made computing personal
items.author: Waldrop, M. Mitchell
items.note: A section headed for 'MIT hackers play Spacewar on the PDP-1' under interactivity for the masses; Spacewar as an on-screen sci-fi adventure and a stockholder demonstration; later notes Rolling Stone's headline.

items.title: Trigger happy: the inner life of videogames
items.author: Poole, Steven
items.note: Chapter 'The Origin of Species': the name's melodrama, duelling spaceships against a model of the night sky, its failure to become mass entertainment, and Bushnell at Utah leading to 1,500 units of Computer Space. Spacewar! at 30.

items.title: Dealers of lightning: Xerox PARC and the dawn of the computer age
items.author: Hiltzik, Michael A
items.note: Chapter 11 'Spacewar' concerns Brand's 1972 Rolling Stone article: its delight at PARC, reaction among traditionalists at Xerox headquarters, half of it on other Bay Area labs, and its spread of PARC's reputation. Spacewar! at 155-162.

items.title: L'Univers des jeux vidéo
items.author: Le Diberder, Alain
items.note: Places Space War beside Kennedy's Moon promise, as a primitive science fiction game and a cult game in the 1960s; Bushnell entered Utah in 1962, with Atari's correct commercial adaptation fifteen years later. Spacewar! at 18.

items.title: Joystick nation: how videogames ate our quarters, won our hearts, and rewired our minds
items.author: Herz, J. C. (Jessie Cameron)
items.note: Calls it the ur-videogame, tells of Russell's friends polishing it on study breaks and the first joypad, copies on every research computer by the mid-1960s, and Computer Space as a variation on it.

items.title: Fumbling the future: how Xerox invented, then ignored, the first personal computer
items.author: Smith, Douglas K.
items.note: Summarises Brand's Rolling Stone article and its thesis on interactive computing, naming Peter Deutsch among those it featured, as part of the PARC story. Spacewar! at 148-149.

items.title: Tools for thought: the people and ideas behind the next computer revolution
items.author: Rheingold, Howard
items.note: Late-night hackers run Spacewar on a rigged PDP-1 using a control panel made from a cigar box; it spreads from MIT to other campus computers, and a figure falls when it is banned and recovers when reinstated.

items.title: Zap!: the rise and fall of Atari
items.author: Cohen, Scott
items.note: Early pages: Russell at MIT writes the program, and a reference to Bushnell. Bill Pitts, who played at Stanford, uses a DEC machine for a commercial version of his own, Galaxy Game, very like it. Spacewar! at 16-18.

items.title: Screen play: the story of video games
items.author: Sullivan, George
items.note: Early history for general readers: a Massachusetts student's program with two dots as spacecraft, buffs spreading it, and Bushnell playing at night in his computer science department, with a quotation from him. Spacewar! at 28-29, 58.

items.title: Genesis II, creation and recreation with computers
items.author: Peterson, Dale
items.note: First-person account by someone who wrote the game: adding a star display, copies spreading to other PDP-1 installations, and a rule against play outside demonstrations; mentions Minnesota Spacewar with invisible rockets. Speaker's name not seen.

items.title: EP.271 - Il primo videogame
items.author: Morroni, Jacopo
items.note: Italian episode on what counts as the first video game; names Spacewar! as the first to spread widely.

items.title: Nascita di un gigante: forme di produzione e consumo dei videogiochi dalle origini al 1999
items.author: Rizzo, Diego
items.note: Italian thesis on the origins of video game production and consumption, following Russell to completion in February 1962 and the spread of the free code across campuses. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 23, 25.

items.title: The History of Video Games (Episode 2) - History's First Video Game(s)
items.author: The History of Video Games
items.in: YouTube, The History of Video Games
items.note: Episode with a segment on Spacewar!, Russell and TMRC.

items.title: Interactive Programming
items.author: Petricek, Tomas
items.note: Book chapter on interactive programming with a titled section 3.1 on Spacewar! as a turn away from batch processing at the start of the 1960s. Spacewar! at section 3.1, from p. 81.

items.title: The multiplayer game: user identity and the meaning of home video games in the United States, 1972-1994
items.author: Impellizeri, Kevin Donald
items.in: Library, Museums and Press - UDSpace (University of Delaware)
items.note: Places Spacewar! among mainframe games used by campus computer clubs: Russell's first version, Smith's Skylark as source, and the Tech Model Railroad Club's collaborative modifications. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 261-262.

items.title: Tila kertojana
items.author: Maalismaa, Matti
items.note: Bachelor's thesis on game space. Takes Spacewar! as a leading candidate for the first represented game space, discusses the star map as both mechanical and narrative via Graetz, and tells Samson's Game Transfer anecdote. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 14, 35.

items.title: Klangwelten digitaler Spiele: Zur Bedeutung von Sound und Musik für Game Design und Forschung
items.author: Redecker, Björn
items.in: Bild und Bit. Studien zur digitalen Medienkultur
items.note: German book on game sound; its game history section dates Spacewar! to Russell's group in 1961, spreading in academic circles from 1962, on the PDP-1. Chapter DOIs 10.1515/9783839473702-014, 10.14361/9783839473702-015.

items.title: The Birth and Development of Sports Video Games From the 1950s to the Early 1980s
items.author: Zhouxiang, Lu
items.note: History of sports video games with a passage on Spacewar! at MIT as a mainframe game and on later variations adding multiple ships, partial damage, scores, mines and stealth.

items.title: Computer Space
items.in: World Video Game Hall of Fame, The Strong National Museum of Play
items.note: Hall of Fame entry describing Spacewar! as the most popular early lab game, Bushnell's encounter with it, the cost of the hardware, and how Computer Space differed.

items.title: Esports no Brasil de 2022: o que torna grande uma organização?
items.author: Oliveira, Gabriel Celestino de
items.note: Undergraduate thesis. Names Spacewar! with Tennis for Two as the first entertainment video games, and tells the Intergalactic Spacewar Olympics at Stanford as the start of esports, with Baumgart's photograph as winner. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 8, 12, 14.

items.title: The New King of the Entertainment Industry? The Unlikely Story of Video Games and the First Amendment
items.author: Walters, Ryan M.
items.publisher: Ohio State University. Moritz College of Law
items.note: Law article. Dates the start of its Two-Dimensional Era from Spacewar! in 1962, describes MIT's creators, the ship duel, four switches and the lack of computing power for a computer opponent, then the space shooter genre. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 34-35.

items.title: Tennis to Space War | Video Game Documentary
items.author: Play History
items.note: Documentary episode on the move from early novelty computer games to Spacewar!.

items.title: AI Lab celebrates 50th anniversary of Intergalactic 'Spacewar!' Olympics
items.author: Udaygiri, Ananya
items.note: Report of SAIL's anniversary event, with 1972 winner Bruce Baumgart present; new games replaced Spacewar! and Rolling Stone subscriptions were again the prize.

items.title: Analogue Reveals new "openFPGA" For Their Pocket Handheld
items.author: Wallace, Anthony
items.note: Describes the PDP-1 and Spacewar! core as the launch title for Analogue's openFPGA programme.

items.title: Analogue Pocket's 1.1 Update Beta Brings Game Libraries, Better Save States, and 3rd Party Cores
items.author: Ehrhardt, Michelle
items.note: Covers the Pocket firmware and the third-party Spacewar! core shipped with it.

items.title: Video Games Have Never Been Global: Resituating Video Game Localization History
items.author: Mandiberg, Stephen
items.note: Moves the origin of game localization back to Spacewar!, treating its migration and adaptation at other sites as localization.

items.title: Deporte y espectáculo en la narrativa de los 'e-sports': el caso de 'League of Legends'
items.author: Martín Muñoz, Diego; Pedrero Esteban, Luis Miguel
items.note: Recounts Spacewar! as built by MIT students to show off the PDP-1, its spread to universities, Galaxy Game as a version of it, and a 1972 Stanford tournament as the first esports event. Spacewar! at 65 and the preceding history section.

items.title: How one immense flaw doomed the real first commercial video game
items.author: Wardrip-Fruin, Noah
items.note: On the star added in April 1962 and its gravity well making strategy possible, and Computer Space failing partly for lack of it. Also at MIT Press Reader as Before Pong, There Was Computer Space.

items.title: APC, August 2021
items.note: Disputes over the first PC game, describing the game as the inspiration for Asteroids and its public-domain code and later ports. Spacewar! at scan leaf 63.

items.title: Ancient History
items.note: Early gaming history from pinball and Tennis for Two to personal computers, Spacewar! and the Magnavox Odyssey.

items.title: Wireframe no. 40 (2 July 2020)
items.note: Treats the game as the first made for a minicomputer, its use as a PDP-1 diagnostic and its later status as a curio. Spacewar! at scan leaf 37.
items.author: Wireframe Magazine

items.title: Replay (Argentina) no. 22
items.note: Argentine feature on the journey started by the game, its circulation among American universities and the students it reached. Spacewar! at scan leaves 10, 12.
items.author: Replay, Revista

items.title: #1 - Décadas de 1940-1960: Nimatron, Tennis for Two e os Pioneiros dos Games
items.note: Portuguese episode with a segment listed as Steve Russell and Spacewar, the MIT revolution.

items.title: 1. Firsts: You're the Alvin
items.note: Episode on videogame firsts in which Glenn discusses Spacewar! as the first computer game.

items.title: Wireframe no. 35 (26 March 2020)
items.note: Discusses the game's influence and the attitudes to software development it fostered, with Russell and the TMRC. Spacewar! at scan leaves 45-46.
items.author: Wireframe Magazine

items.title: Elektronik Spor Oyunlarında Siber Zorbalık
items.author: ÇAVDAR, Bilal
items.note: Turkish thesis on esports with a figure of Russell and the PDP-1 and an account of Spacewar by Russell, Graetz and Wiitanen. Spacewar! at PDF p. 28.

items.title: La réitération nostalgique, humoristique et critique des motifs de la guerre froide dans Fallout 4
items.author: Engel, Hugo
items.note: Describes Spacewar! on the PDP-1 and its simulated stellar gravity, citing Triclot to tie its theme to Cold War space culture and the space games that followed. Spacewar! at PDF pp. 20, 47-48.

items.title: Playing at Narratology: Digital Media as Narrative Theory
items.author: Punday, Daniel
